utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I intimated last day that Ambassador Vollebaek is available today, and I had asked whether perhaps the last witness might be able to -- I think I used the phrase wrapped around this witness. Ambassador Vollebaek is here now, and I would propose, with the Court's permission, to proceed with Ambassador Vollebaek and then continue thereafter with the continuation of the previous witness, if that meets with the Court's approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think technically you need leave to call Mr. Vollebaek because he wasn't on your original list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Then I seek oral -- this is an oral application to call Ambassador Vollebaek at this time. I do believe that his materials were served quite some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The statement was disclosed and it was disclosed in B/C/S by the 15th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Accordingly, there is no prejudice in calling him now and leave will be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's only available today, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That was my understanding, however, upon his arrival a little while ago, apparently his flight schedule is not quite as tight. He could continue on until tomorrow, if necessary, but having made arrangements with the last witness, who is now not here, I don't want to waste a moment's court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We will call this witness and deal with him, if at all possible, today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That would be wonderful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness with take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat, Mr. Vollebaek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Ryneveld:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador Vollebaek, I understand, sir, that you started your diplomatic service in the Norwegian diplomatic service in 1973?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also right, sir, that you became the Norwegian Minister of Foreign Affairs in 1997 and served in that capacity until March of the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, while you were the Norwegian Minister of Foreign Affairs, did you serve in any other office with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. In the capacity as Norwegian Foreign Minister, I was chairman in office of the OSCE during the year 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your present function today, sir, is?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I am Norway's ambassador to the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to ask -- back you up to the year of 1993. Did you hold any particular office at that time in relation to the international conference of former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. From the 1st of June, if I recall correctly, until the end of 1993, I was what was called deputy co-chairman of the international conference on former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while engaged in that capacity, sir, did you have any involvement in negotiations between particular governments?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. My main responsibility during those months was to negotiate, or try to negotiate, I should rather say, a settlement between the government of the Republic of Croatia and the government of the so-called Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of those negotiations or attempted negotiations, as you phrase it, did you have any dealings with the accused in these proceedings, then President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Not a lot, but we thought that Belgrade had some influence on the Republic of Krajina and so we referred to Belgrade from time to time. Then Foreign Minister Jovanovic I met with on several occasions, and I also met with President Milosevic. At least I remember one meeting with him in connection with -- we tried to set up secret negotiations in Norway between the Serbs and the Croats. I guess we -- at that time we were somewhat inspired by other Norwegian colleagues that had achieved something in the Middle East and we thought we could do something similar in this connection. And at that time I met with President Milosevic for him to put pressure on the Serbs in Knin to go along with my proposal for these negotiations in Norway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Milosevic at that time appear to be willing to assist you in achieving your objective?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: He did. This was in the early fall, if I recall this correctly. I think the meeting in Norway took place in November, so this must have been -- or maybe October. So this must have been in September, early October. And I went to Belgrade and had a meeting with him, as I said, and at that time, the government of Croatia had battles going on both with the Muslims in Bosnia and at the same time then with the Serbs in Knin, in the Krajina Republic. And I asked for his help, and he said that he would assist me because he felt that it would be difficult for the Croats to fight two fronts at the same time, and according to him, it was more important to fight the Muslims than the Serb -- the Croats should be able to fight the Muslims and in order for the Croats to fight the Muslims, the Serbs should kind of step back and let the Croats fight the Muslims. And his statement, as I still recall very vividly and as I thought of sometimes during 1999 was that the reason why he did this, that we could not have a Muslim republic in Europe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you've already explained it, but what did you understand him to mean when he said something about not having two fronts?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, he indicated to me that he was impressed, as I understood it, with the Croat military power, but in spite of the fact that the Croats were good fighters, good military, to have two fronts at the same time would be too much for them. And as I understood him, he thought it was important for all of us, I guess he implied, to fight the Muslims. And then in order to -- to let the Croats concentrate, so to say, on the Muslims, he would ask the government in Knin to participate in the talks that we were going to have in Norway and then, for the time being at least, not pursue military activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Ambassador Vollebaek, in 1993, what was Milosevic's position? Like, what position did he hold with what government?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall, he had the same position as he had in 1999; he was President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you go to him in order to attempt to persuade other -- other governments or other entities to come to Norway to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, we were under the impression that the government in Knin was heavily supported, strongly supported, by the government in Belgrade and then, in casu, then President Milosevic. We knew that members of the Knin government went to Belgrade very often, and we thought and presumed that President Milosevic had a strong influence on the government in Knin. And since the representatives of the Knin government then went to Norway for these talks, later on I was strengthened in my belief that there was an influence from Belgrade on the government of Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because they showed up at the --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: They showed up, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Sir, just to take you to more recent times, we've heard in these proceedings considerable evidence from various individuals about the OSCE, but as I understand it, sir, you were the -- you were the chairman of the OSCE. You were the chief executive officer, as it were, in that capacity, were you, of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. We had a secretary-general, or the OSCE has a secretary-general, which is an employee, but the chairman in office is a politically elected function. It changes every year, so it's held by a Foreign Ministry of one of the member countries for one calendar year, and Norway had been selected then to hold this position for the year of 1999. And since I happened to be the foreign minister at that time, it was my task to be the chairman in office of the organisation for that year. There is -- there is a troika system, which means that you start in -- as a member of the troika the year before and you continue the year after. So I started working with the -- with the issues already in 1998. At that time, it was Professor Geremek, the Foreign Minister of Poland, who held the office as chairman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So you spent a year sort of getting ready to take office the following year?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you hold office, and then you sort of hold office for a year to assist the newcomer so that there's, I take it --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Continuity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- continuity in the position. I understand. But during 1999 when you were the chairman, how many member states were there? How many countries were there that made up the OSCE? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: There are 54 members. I think there still are 54 members of the OSCE. In 1999, Yugoslavia was suspended, so their chair was vacant, so only 53 countries were present in the organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was Yugoslavia suspended? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That happened because of the Balkan conflict and the decision by the organisation to suspend it due to the fact that Yugoslavia did not live up to its obligations as a member of the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, have they now been reinstated?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: They have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've already made reference, sir, to the previous chairman, Geremek. Was there, in 1998 while you were already working with Geremek, were you aware of a special mandate with respect to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. The OSCE had by itself, so to say, a mandate for the peaceful settlement of conflicts, for democratisation, for human rights in Europe, but in the dealing with the Kosovo conflict, there were, if I recall correctly, two Resolutions by the Security Council. If my memory doesn't fail me, I think it was 1160 and 1199, but anyway, those Resolutions gave or asked the OSCE to take upon themselves to try to find a peaceful settlement to the Kosovo conflict. And in order to fulfil that request by the Security Council, there were negotiations between the government of Yugoslavia and the OSCE, and there was an agreement signed between Foreign Minister Geremek, and I think it was signed by Foreign Minister Jovanovic of Yugoslavia in October 1998 that should then lead up to the presence of OSCE in Yugoslavia and specifically then in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware, I take it, of a document known as the Holbrooke agreement? Is this in substitution for or in addition to or totally separate from what has been colloquially referred to as the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: My understanding is that the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement should be in support of the role of the OSCE and of the peaceful settlement. I didn't always feel it that way, I must admit, when I spoke to Mr. Milosevic about it, because when I -- well, the formal basis for our presence was, of course, the OSCE agreement, and we had a mandate on that basis. But at the same time, it was this additional agreement, as you said, the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement, that, I must admit, I've never seen, but it came up in the conversations I had with Mr. Milosevic, and -- but it came up in a way that when I asked for something, when I demanded something of him, he claimed that this was without the agreement he had with Mr. Holbrooke. So -- and I could not verify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, remind me of this: We have the OSCE agreement in evidence, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We do, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could remind me sometime what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I know we have the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement. That I remember. In October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There is a document, and we'll find it in just a moment, that's actually signed by Geremek and that's the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Judge Kwon kindly reminds me. It's tab 94. As I remembered, the Milosevic agreement is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I believe it's in the binder of materials constituting Exhibit 94 that were introduced through General Drewienkiewicz. I just don't know what tab number without reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The answer is it's tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the other agreement is tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I thought they would be fairly early in the binder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of quick questions, sir. We know that the OSCE was made up of 54 member states, et cetera, et cetera. What function, what particular issues or interests did the OSCE attempt to safeguard during its -- during its mandate?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: The OSCE was following up, so to say, of the so-called CSE, the conference on Cooperation and Security in Europe, and that conference was then made into an organisation, a permanent body, which was the OSCE. The conference was based on the Helsinki treaty of 1975. It was established during the Cold War as an organisation working with disarmament, with the human rights, trying to pursue efforts for democracy, minorities. So there was a whole range, actually, of - what shall I say? - activities in order to seek a peaceful change from a totalitarian system in then eastern and central Europe and into a democratic system for the whole of Europe. And at the same time, as I said, strongly involved in disarmament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1999, during your chairmanship of the OSCE, did you have any discussions with Mr. Milosevic, among others, about the role that the OSCE might play in the Kosovo conflict? And if so, what kind of reception did you get from Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: You said 1999, during my year as chairman in office?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. I had several meetings with him. As I recall it, I think I had three meetings and I had some telephone conversations. Since Kosovo was, as I saw it at that time, the main task of the OSCE - we had a number of other tasks at the same time but the Kosovo conflict had become such a hot issue, a very serious issue - I felt that I had to concentrate a lot of my efforts as chairman in office of the OSCE on precisely Kosovo. And for that reason, I decided to go to Belgrade early, and I think my -- in my term as chairman. And I think my first meeting with then President Milosevic was on the 11th of January in 1999, when we then discussed the work that we were going to do, the various activities that we were going to do. At that time, if I again recall correctly, some Serbs had been abducted or hijacked, kidnapped by Kosovo Albanians, so that became a very important issue, trying to release those -- and that was maybe my main task during that visit instead of preparing for the ordinary work that the OSCE should be doing. We had established what was called the Kosovo Verification Mission. I understand that you have had witnesses earlier that dealt with that. And my next meeting was 21st or something of January, and that was to discuss the expulsion of Ambassador Walker. Ambassador Walker was the head, as you well know, of the Kosovo Verification Mission, and President Milosevic, and I suppose the government, whatever, had decided to declare Ambassador Walker persona non grata. There was unacceptable to us. It was, as I saw it, a violation of the agreement we had with the government, and I had to try to stop the expulsion, and I -- he was not expelled. And then my last meeting with Mr. Milosevic was on the 1st of March, if I again recall correctly. At that time, the Rambouillet talks, the talks had -- were under way. I think there was a period, a kind of a lapse in the talks, and I went to Belgrade to see if we could try to convince Mr. Milosevic and the government and to pursue the negotiations as we wanted them to pursue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get into some of those meetings that you've just outlined for us with some more specificity. Maybe I should back you up just for a moment. Did you also have any meetings with Mr. Milosevic in 1998, prior to taking on the role as chairman personally?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think the first meeting I had as Norwegian Foreign Minister was in April of 1998, and at that time I knew that I was going to be the chairman of OSCE for the next year so we discussed, obviously, that role and that function and then we discussed the normal -- whatever foreign ministers discuss with the heads of states, and specifically, of course, the very serious situation in Kosovo and in the Balkans in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should ask you, sir, what was Mr. Milosevic's view on the role of the KVM? Was he initially eager to have them present?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: My understanding was that he never liked KVM. I guess he was against an international presence in Kosovo in general. And KVM was supposed to be a larger group than -- you have had something earlier that was called KDOM. I must admit that I'm not very certain about the mandate of that group, but anyway, KVM was going -- it was not an armed group, it was a civilian force, but it -- I think we aimed at having something like 2.000 people so it would be a more -- their presence would be more felt. And it was my understanding that he was not very keen on that, but it was accepted and the first meeting I had with him on the 11th of January, as I said, he accepted the agreement, of course, that was signed between his foreign minister and Foreign Minister Geremek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, without getting into specifics of the meetings that you have had - and we'll get back to those in a moment - I'm going to ask you now to retrospectively look at the collective meetings you've had with President Milosevic, as he then was, and can you tell the Court, if you would, please, what impression you formed about his authority or lack of it.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think Mr. Milosevic had a lot of authority. He -- his presence was very much felt when he was present, and at least I was left with the impression that he was a man in control and in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during some of these meetings, were any of his other senior assistants or officials or ministers present?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. In all meetings except for the meeting that you referred to earlier in 1993, I cannot recall to have had any meetings with him alone. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I had members of my staff with me, and he had, as I recall it, a number of his officials, other political members, military leaders with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met with Milosevic and his other senior ministers, were you able to form any impression as to who ultimately made decisions? Did the ministers make decisions or did Milosevic make decisions or could you see who made decisions?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, this is, of course, based on impression. I was never present in any of the internal discussions that the government of Yugoslavia had, but in -- as I said, in all the meetings I had with him together with other people, he was the one that mainly spoke. He was the one that mainly drew conclusions. And in some of the meetings we had, for instance, in Kosovo with -- I guess his name was Andjelkovic or something like that, his representative in Kosovo, there was no doubt that everything was referred back to Belgrade. I mean, there was nothing that they could decide without having this confirmed. And when we spoke and they spoke about Belgrade, I was, anyway, under the impression that we talked about Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Sir, you made reference a few moments ago to the first of a series of meetings. Perhaps we can talk first about the meeting in January of 1999. I believe the date you gave was the 11th of January. Perhaps -- what -- I'm sorry. The subject matter of the meeting on the 11th of January, I believe you mentioned, referred to some VJ soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's right. Well, it was supposed to be an ordinary meeting, preparing for the work that we were going to do, but just before I arrived, some -- some VJ soldiers had been abducted by Kosovo Albanians, and this made an outcry in Belgrade and this was the issue that was brought up. And we were asked, or maybe even more than asked, demanded to see if we could release -- have them released. So we had a lot of activities with reference to that, trying to get those released, which we succeeded in having. So that became one of the main issues in addition to more the ordinary discussion on how to deal with the role of KVM in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly to say that your organisation was involved and successful in assisting in the prisoner exchange or the VJ soldier exchange?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is my belief, yes, that we did so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you have subsequent conversations after the 15th of January, after Racak, with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. On -- when the Racak massacre happened, of course that was a very serious incident which we took very seriously, and based on what Mr. Milosevic found as the inappropriate reaction of Ambassador Walker, he or the government decided to declare Ambassador Walker persona non grata and wanted to expel him. In that situation, I knew that the whole KVM mission would fall apart. I mean, one could not expel the head of the mission without looking at the whole mission. And for that reason, I had immediately a telephone conversation with the Foreign Minister Jovanovic to discuss it with him, asked for a meeting with President Milosevic, and I was -- I had this meeting on the -- I think it was on the 21st of January, and the -- my objective was to have this decision undone or changed. It was unacceptable, and I said it was a violation of the agreement we had. It said in the agreement, if I recall correctly, it states quite clearly that it is up to me, as chairman in office of the OSCE, to appoint or fire the head of the KVM mission. This has nothing to do with the country in which they are serving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. And just so that we're clear, you had appointed Ambassador Walker as the head of the KVM; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. Or it was Professor Geremek as chairman in office, but it was the chairman in office of the OSCE who should appoint him according to the agreement that was signed between Jovanovic and Geremek, and it was also up to the chairman in office to tell the head of the KVM to step down, if he so desired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your view was that this was something that was in your mandate, not -- not the mandate of the country that was being observed.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct. And more so, I don't think it was only my view but I think it said so in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Was there a further discussion with the accused about Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. We had a number of discussions, I would say, on Mr. Walker, and Mr. Milosevic found -- I mean, he disliked his appearance, to my understanding, a lot, and he found that his reaction after the Racak massacre was inappropriate. His comments had been not in accordance with his position, I think he said, and that was the reason then why he wanted him expelled. And he offered, if I recall correctly, offered to have a Norwegian as the head of the KVM. He asked me, "Why couldn't we have a Norwegian as the head of the KVM?" And I said this was not up to him to select the head of the KVM. So we had a long discussion that day, or even into the early night, I would say, about KVM and Ambassador Walker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador Vollebaek, I'm going to wait between your questions and -- or your answers to my questions because of translation. Because we both speak the same language, I'm afraid that we haven't been allowing for the translators, so I'll pause.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll try to behave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. It's my fault. Now, did you ultimately resolve this apparent conflict concerning Ambassador Walker?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. We solved it in the sense that it was decided, according to Mr. Milosevic, by the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to freeze the expulsion. We had a long discussion on different phraseology and conditions, and I could not accept any conditions because there were no -- as I saw it, there were no conditions that were -- he was not entitled to impose any conditions. And at the end of the conversation, he proposed or accepted that there should be a freeze of the expulsion, unconditional freeze, and that was then put forward, as I understood it, to the government of FRY. And I, of course, also had to consult with the members, the troika members of the OSCE and also with the Contact Group members if this was acceptable to them. And it was acceptable to my side, and I was later then called back to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Belgrade, and the foreign minister told me that the government had accepted that this -- this freezing of the expulsion should take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The result of that was Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That Ambassador Walker could continue as head of KVM until the withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of these negotiations, was there any discussion about forensic -- independent forensic examinations of the bodies found at Racak?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. This was an issue that I think primarily was raised by the KVM itself because they had the mandate and the duty to look into these incidents that happened on the ground. As I recall it, Mr. Milosevic refused. I think they had some local Serb forensic expert to look into it first. Then, in order to make this kind of international, he asked, if I recall correctly, a group from Belarus, but we insisted that there should be someone from the OSCE side accepted that we had chosen. We had a long discussion on this, and -- but the end was that there was a Finnish group, headed by, if I remember correctly, Dr. Ranta, that was allowed in. But again, if my memory doesn't fail me, they came in almost a week after the massacre happened. So they came in quite late and they complained about that. They said that of course the bodies had been moved, things had happened. So they were criticising that they had not been able to come earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the result of the negotiation was that the Finnish team was also permitted to come in and participate in this forensic examination although they complained it was much too late.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's right, but they did come in and they did make a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I just want to back up and just ask a question that I'd forgotten to put to you earlier, sir. You referred earlier to a meeting with someone, and I believe you mentioned the word "Andjelkovic." Is that Zoran Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. My memory may fail me, but as -- I cannot confirm his first name, but as I recall, he was the local representative of the federal government or the government of Belgrade in Pristina. So he was my main interlocutor, a kind of host, when I visited Pristina. And I had meetings with him, some with him in his capacity as representative but also then as head of the council that they had with representatives of various -- kind of an elected body. So he -- as I understood him, he was then appointed by Belgrade as a caretaker governor, whatever, of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the gentleman you said that from time to time would say that he'd have to check with Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by that, you understood him to mean Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm at paragraph 12, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your meetings with the accused, you said apart from that one meeting, I believe in 1993, he always had other people with him?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And including some of the people you've already mentioned, were there any military personnel, generals or anything like that, in his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. company during your meetings?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. As I recall it, I think there were generals or military personnel in all the meetings. Well, I stated I had three meetings with him before -- in 1999 before the military activities of the Kosovo conflict, the bombing started, and as I recall it, there were military personnel present in all these three meetings, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've told us earlier that it appeared that it was the accused that made decisions, or at least that was your impression of it. Did that also include discussions concerning matters where the military were present?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those discussions sometimes involve military matters?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, they did, to the extent that we were talking about the presence, the military presence, in Kosovo. We were talking about what we saw as attacks or -- what should I say -- activities against the KVM by the military that we said was unacceptable to us. So -- and there were also then activities along the borderline with Macedonia. So there were several issues without me actually remembering each concrete issue, but military issues and activities were discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Milan Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I cannot say I know him, but I met him in the presence of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he present at some or all of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: My impression is that he was present at all, but I may be wrong. But he was present at some of the meetings, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you understand his role to be when you met him? What was his title?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, at that time, he was President of the Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your meetings, you discussed, I take it, the international observer role in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, because the main task of the OSCE at that time was the KVM, the Kosovo Verification Mission. We demanded, according to the agreement we had with the government of Yugoslavia, was then to seek a peaceful settlement, to ask or to try to make possible the return of the number of refugees that had left Kosovo. So these -- how to facilitate that return, how to seek or how to start, maybe, negotiations between the government of Belgrade and representatives of the Kosovo Albanian population was, of course, the main task for me and the main topic that we had during our conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your negotiations or discussions, was an international military presence one of the topics at any stage?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. At least in the conversation we had on the 1st of March. Because since we saw that the situation did not improve, it, rather, deteriorated in Kosovo, as I mentioned, KVM was an observer group without any military force and we saw that we could not fulfil the mandate that we had, the only way that we thought that we could pursue our activities was with a military presence. And this was also discussed during the Rambouillet talks and was a part of the Rambouillet proposal. And so I brought up and pressed for Mr. Milosevic's acceptance of a military presence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was that suggestion received?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not very favourably. He was very upset for many reasons. He stated clearly that Kosovo was an integral part of Serbia, as he said, that -- I mean, it was unheard-of that you had international troops, military forces on the soil of a sovereign state. In addition to that, since Yugoslavia was suspended from the OSCE, he -- he saw no reason why OSCE should impose anything like this on him. And he compared, actually, this military presence to the -- to the Soviet invasion of Prague because he said that -- well, he -- as I said, he was rather upset, and he said that he would not accept my proposal. And he said that Yugoslavia had stood up against Stalin, and they had stood up against Breschnev, and they should also stand up against Mr. Vollebaek. So he -- I had a nice comparison there. And I tried to tell him that this wasn't by invitation. I mean, he was still then the president, and it would be under -- I mean, upon invitation. It was nothing compared to either what Stalin did or what the Soviet Union did in Prague in 1968, but that was how he felt it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you if you would explain for the Court, please, what you meant earlier when you indicated that one of the reasons that you discussed an international military presence was because the OSCE was unable to fulfil its mandate. What did you mean by that? What problems did you have as civilians?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, as -- as I said, I visited Kosovo three times before the war broke out, and I saw, I think specifically my second visit, I saw that there was a great trust in KVM from the population in Kosovo. They had seen improvement in their situation, much more security. Some villagers had returned to their villages. I visited, myself, both posts manned by Yugoslav military personnel and KLA personnel and saw that we had a mediating role, we had a role of a buffer, and there was a rather optimistic atmosphere, I would say. This was then in late January of 1999. And the morale among the KVM observers, monitors, was also quite high because they felt they had a role to play. Then when I came back in early March, that situation was totally changed because there had been a number of incidents. There had been an increased military -- Yugoslav military presence, in violation of the agreement that we had. People had started fleeing again or leaving their homes. You had attacks on members of the KVM. And the local population felt that we didn't do anything for them. I mean, they had lost a lot of confidence in us. And all this resulted in the fact that we could not do what we were supposed to do; starting negotiations, facilitating return of refugees to the country. I mean, new people were leaving. And it became quite clear to me that in order for us to do what we were supposed to do also with respect to democracy building, with respect to the free press, with respect to a number of the activities that we were supposed to do, this could not be done without the military presence that could actually hold the military factions apart from each other. Because you had, as is well known, the KLA, which also had military activities, and with the Yugoslav military activities, the local population was caught in between, and that was impossible for us to do anything or to avoid this because we had -- we were unarmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now, during the course of your discussions, did you hear the accused indicate to you about the potential for ethnic makeup of Kosovo, what groups might be able to reside in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. He always talked about a multi-ethnic Kosovo, and I guess he charged me and us with being too pro-Albanian and not taking into consideration the Serb population, the Roma population, the various other groups that you had in Kosovo. And he -- so he was very strongly committed then to, as he said, to a multi-ethnic Kosovo. I told him that we also were concerned with the other groups. I had a number of meetings with representatives of the Serb opposition, for instance, representatives of the Serb groups in Kosovo, and we were discussing their situation. And I gave clear instructions to KVM also to look into whatever incidents where the Serb population and the Roma people were under attack from the Kosovo Albanian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In discussions about these ethnic groups, were there any conditions attached to their residents in Kosovo in terms of majority of individuals and respecting decisions of the majority?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Could you elaborate a little bit more on that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase. I'll rephrase. Did you find out from the accused who he deemed to be the majority ethnic group in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm not certain that we actually, to my recollection, actually discussed what was the majority as such. He felt very strongly that the Albanians would have to comply with the -- with the Serb rule, so to say, because that was, of course, as he saw it, Kosovo was a part of Serbia, Kosovo was an integral part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: And he refused -- well, I would not say refused, but he did not want to discuss a great deal autonomy. We were playing with a number of models where Kosovo could have a greater deal of autonomy and referring to earlier constitutions and things like that. But he was very adamant that since Kosovo was an integral part of Serbia, the -- in spite of the fact that at some stage he would accept the Albanian language maybe and some cultural identifications, this was a part of Serbia and as such they would have to accept the Serb overall rule, so to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. All right. During the course of your discussions, did you raise with the accused the alleged atrocities that you had heard about from your observers, and did you discuss those with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Certainly. This was, of course, issues that we brought up every time, and not least when we had the meeting on the 21st of January. The Racak massacre was a very prominent item, precisely because -- well, it had happened, and the OSCE had made a quite strong statement, I think it was on the 16th of January, condemning the massacre, and we asked for an investigation, and also then since the consequence of this was the attempt to expel Ambassador Walker, this Racak massacre was very much an issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to spend valuable court time revisiting a number of documents that have already been entered in in tab 94, but are you aware whether or not the OSCE would provide daily reports about their observations and reports about incidents that they had witnessed or their members had witnessed?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Certainly. They made -- I would think they made daily reports. At least, they made reports, I think they were on a daily basis, that were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sent back to Vienna, to the OSCE headquarters, about whatever happened, and also about the Racak massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we -- we started at 9.30. I'll continue. I thought we were coming up to the break. You referred, sir, to three meetings earlier in yourself, on the 11th of January, the 21st of January, and the 1st of March. You've discussed those. I'm going to take you now to the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a telephone conversation with the accused on that date?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At that time, the Paris talks, as I think they were called at that time, had broken up, and it became more and more evident that we were heading towards an armed conflict. And I felt very strongly, as the chairman of the OSCE, that it was in my -- it was my duty to try to do whatever I could to avoid an armed conflict. And I had a conversation with Secretary-General Solana, who was at that time Secretary-General of NATO, and I said to him that I would like to try one more time if I could convince Mr. Milosevic to go along with some talks and allow a military presence and so that we could see if we could avoid the military conflict that we understood was coming. I did not know -- as you will recall as happened, the bombing started that evening. I did not know at that time, but I knew that it was growing near. And I made a telephone conversation to him, to Mr. Milosevic around early -- or late morning/early afternoon, if I recall correctly, and tried to explain to him the serious situation, and also told him that I was available if I could do something. Of course, he disagreed with my view, he disagreed with my proposal. I explained to him that the situation had deteriorated to such an extent that it was difficult for us to see any solution. As you may know, the KVM had withdrawn earlier, just some days earlier, again as a result of the breakdown of the negotiations and the security situation that became increasingly deteriorating for the KVM monitors and also the lack of possibility of fulfilling the mandate, as I mentioned earlier. And we saw then a build-up of military personnel in Kosovo after this. There had been an exodus of refugees. A number of refugees had left, there was pressure on the border towards Macedonia and Albania, and we had reports from UNHCR and ICRC after the -- that KVM had left about the situation that was deteriorating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you called him.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps you could outline for us to the best of your recollection the points that you discussed with Mr. Milosevic on that occasion. You've told us that -- did you tell him about seeing the build-up of troops, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's right. I had seen this when I was there in March, on the 1st of March. It was -- as I said, it was a different atmosphere on the 1st of March compared to my visit in late January. And I had then seen people leaving with their belongings, and those members of KVM with whom I was travelling, they were quite concerned because they said that this was a new situation, they hadn't seen this lately, so they were very concerned about this. We had -- the military presence was very prevalent, and clearly a build-up compared to what I had seen earlier. We saw also fire. I could not detect exactly what that fire was, but later on that was confirmed by, among others, ICRC and I think also UNHCR, but anyway ICRC and the KVM, for that matter in March before they withdrew, that houses were being set ablaze.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps I can take some of these points one at a time. In relation to the build-up of military forces, et cetera, did you complain about that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I said that this was in violation of the agreement. To that, Mr. Milosevic said that they were there to protect me, which I didn't think was necessary, to say it mildly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mention, sir, that the reports were that people were fleeing with their belongings. Did you also get reports about whether they were congregating once they fled?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. We were in touch, of course, with the -- well, both KVM were following them and seeing what happened to them, but also we were in touch with the government of Macedonia. It was very concerned with the situation because a number of people came into Macedonia. The same happened in Albania but maybe the problem was even greater on the border with Macedonia. But again, when I confronted Mr. Milosevic with that, he said that they were just picnicking, so I shouldn't be concerned. They were just on a trip, having picnic. I think I said that it was strange to have a picnic with all your belongings on a tractor trailer, but that was the answer I got. And the same with the burning houses, actually. He told me that it was nonsense that there were any houses burning. They were only straw that KLA or the Kosovo Albanians put the fire to -- put fire to in order to pretend that houses were burning. I said that I had seen some of this myself and I had credible reports from international observers that this was happening, and I said that in response to his statement that I was watching too much CNN, because he said that I was fooled by CNN. And I then said that I had seen this myself on some occasion, or one occasion, and then I had also had reports about the same events or incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you comment on the way these people were being handled and what -- did you give any advice to the accused as to what he ought to do?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Certainly. I -- I told him, as I said, that we had -- he should return to the negotiating table, he should allow military presence in order for us to keep the military groups apart so that the refugees could return, and he had to stop violating the agreement we had and to stop harassing people. So -- but according to him then, nothing wrong was happening, so it was difficult to give him advice because there was -- I mean, according to him, I was wrong and there was no reason for him or his government to change the activities or the behaviour with respect to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hold out any hope for further negotiation?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: If he complied with my requests, yes. If we could have a military presence, if he was willing to open up again for talks, I said that since I had spoken earlier to Secretary-General Solana, I knew that we could stop the NATO activities, and I knew also that I had the full support of the OSCE troika and the Contact Group in this. But -- but he kind of discarded me completely. He put me off and said that I was wrong. So I had -- the only thing I could say at the end of the conversation was that I was sorry that his vision of the world or the conflict was very different from mine and that there was nothing I could do at that stage but that I was there, I was available, so he could call me any time if he changed his mind, which he didn't do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you any interest in continued discussions?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll back up to something that you referred sort of in passing to in order to explain a previous conversation. You mentioned that -- something to the effect of, "As you know, we withdrew the KVM on an earlier date." Can you tell us approximately when that was and why that was?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It happened between the 19th and the 20th, if I recall correctly, of March. I think it started -- the decision was taken on the 19th of March and I think it started early morning of the 20th of March. As I said, the situation for KVM had deteriorated very much. We felt that there was a threat to the security of the monitors, and at the same time, they could not fulfil their tasks and their mandate. I had been under some pressure for some time to withdraw KVM, partly, I think, because of the threatened security for the various monitors, that some countries felt that their citizens were not protected well enough and this became political issues in some of the countries, as I understood it. And also that the mandate was not fulfilled. People started asking, "Why are you there?" We had very much Srebrenica in mind, and I think we felt very strongly that we could not be in a position where we repeated a situation where you had an international presence standing by, idly watching atrocities happening. This was very much in our mind when we were discussing and seeing what we could do in Kosovo. At the same time, I also thought that the situation for the civilians would deteriorate if we withdrew. I wanted them to be there as long as possible, that I could in any way defend having them there, because still I thought and hoped that they could do something. And as long as the negotiations in Paris went on, I thought that there still was hope that we could change the attitude of Mr. Milosevic, his government, and might have then an agreement on which we could base our activities. So I would not -- I wouldn't like to withdraw before I really had to. But when the negotiations in Paris broke down and the -- we had some incidents that involved KVM people, that they were attacked by Serb military groups or Serb paramilitary groups maybe, but anyway, they were under -- we had reports that they were attacked or harassed might be the right English word, and I knew, after having been to Kosovo myself, that the trust of KVM was in danger because we could not fulfil the mandate. Then after then consultation with the troika members of the OSCE, and I think I consulted with all the members of the Contact Group, at least some of the major members of the Contact Group, I decided to pull out. It was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. also on advice of Ambassador Walker, who was head, as you know, of the KVM. And we had had this discussion before. Ambassador Walker might have wanted to withdraw even a little bit earlier, but when he then stated very clearly that he could not guarantee the security of the members of the monitoring group any longer, I could not, sitting in Oslo, take the responsibility of keeping people in place. So that was the reason why we decided that they should withdraw, and the withdrawal then took place on the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, immediately after the KVM withdrawal on the 19th, 20th of March, 1999, did you personally witness large movements of refugees out of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That was a little bit later. This was after the bombing had started. I do not recall the dates, but it must have been early April or -- yes, after the bombing had started. I visited Albania and Macedonia, and we had set up -- the OSCE was then in Macedonia, and we provided the UNHCR and some of the other organisations with material, cars to help them handling the refugees. And I visited a couple of refugee camps and had discussions with the Macedonian government on the handling of refugees in Macedonia. In Albania, I was standing at the border crossing when the refugees came, and I must admit, Your Honours, that I have never seen so many tractors in my whole life as I saw that morning. There were an endless line of tractors with whole families on them. And it was, I think, one of the most moving movements in my life when you stand at the border crossing and meet people that have been fleeing for -- well, some for hours because they didn't come that far away but some for some days, and telling stories about how they -- well, of how they had to flee because their house had been taken over by people that came to their apartments or houses and said that they should -- they should leave, or they came back from -- some people said they came back from their evening stroll and their house was occupied. And others then had been more evicted from their houses forcibly, but there were all kinds of very strong stories. I don't speak Serbian, I don't speak Albanian, but I had interpreters who told me this. And then seeing also the situation with the help that was given. The system of assistance was very important. And one of the things that we did was to take down the names and addresses. We had -- we were the third checkpoint, so to say. The first was a bottle of water, the second was a piece of bread, and the third was to take down the names and addresses. Because one of the last things, apparently, that the Serb authorities did before they left Kosovo was to take away all their pieces of identity, even the number, the licence plates on the tractors were cut or clipped off or -- so that they should have no evidence of where they belonged. And so we saw it as our main task to make sure that we knew where these people were, where did they come from, so that they could tell that immediately and we could take that down. And I was, I will admit, being then, in addition to being chairman of the OSCE, I was also foreign minister of a NATO country, as you recall, Your Honours, NATO was responsible for the bombing, of course, and I was somewhat nervous that these people would charge me with being at least one of the culprits. And none of them said anything about -- blamed NATO for the bombing of the country. And they said they did not flee because of the bombs - that was not a problem for them - but fled because their houses were taken over by Serbs, military or non-military groups, and that they had been told to leave, and they were forced to leave. So there was absolutely no complaining. And I think personally that, in spite of the fact that we had, of course, a number of discussions about the withdrawal of KVM when we did withdraw, the fact that we did not stand idly by and watch atrocities happening made the population trust us so that we could move in very soon after the conflict, after the war. And I visited also Kosovo after the war and met with people that cheered and greeted us, both as a member of NATO but also then as chairman of the OSCE because we had taken such a very clear stand on the atrocities that we saw coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One further question about your visit. Did you later return to Kosovo and notice what had happened to various houses or villages or -- are you able to give the Court a firsthand -- what you saw firsthand about what had happened to the Albanian villages?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think I visited Kosovo twice after the war, and we were very concerned with the situation at that time also for the Serb minority. So during my first visit, I had a meeting with Patriarch Pavle in Pec, which was the head of the Serbian Orthodox church, and I had also decided that I would like to go to Decani, which is a very famous Orthodox monastery, and stay over night as a kind of symbol of solidarity with whoever was citizen of Kosovo, and I did that. On the way to Decani -- well, in several places you saw the results, but on the way to Decani, I still remember that there was a whole village where all the roofs were off, and it was obvious that this was not due to bombing but it was fire or -- I'm not an expert on explosives but it was obvious that this came from the ground and not from the air because the interior of the house was being burned off or destroyed. And all the evidence that I received was that this had happened to Kosovo Albanian houses by Serbs, military or paramilitary or whatever, during that period. I also visited with one of the Orthodox bishops a mass grave where there were about, if I recall correctly, 18 bodies. This -- that grave had not been opened yet, so -- but there was one lady that came and thought that her relatives were buried there, and we had -- she was looking then for identification, and there was a process of opening that grave, and we had a discussion with the bishop about the responsibility of the Serbs and how we could now bridge gaps and ask for forgiveness and things that become important in a process of reconciliation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move to a totally different topic now, if I may, Ambassador, if you've had an opportunity to fully answer the questions earlier. During the course of your chairmanship, did you have meetings with people other than the accused? Did you meet, for example, with leaders of the Kosovar Albanians or the KLA or did you participate in any liaison meetings between the accused and some of these representatives?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: In my period there was no meeting between Mr. Milosevic and Kosovo Albanians that I was present in, but I had a number of meetings with Kosovo Albanian leaders. I met with Mr. Rugova who was then one of the more prominent leaders already at that time of the Kosovo Albanian community. I met with him on several occasions. I -- I met also with a number of others. I must admit, Your Honours, that I do not recall all the names. I met with Mr. Sosa in Albania, and I met with what I guess we thought was the head of the KLA, Mr. Hashim Thaci, but that was in Oslo in June, I think it must have been, so it was after the war had started. June of 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: June of 1999.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. I met with him when we were talking about what should happen after the war and how also KLA would have to participate in a peaceful settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this would be after the conflict --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- had been completed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: As I recall, I had no meeting with the KLA before 24th of March, 1999. We thought that some of the political leaders we met with had links to KLA, but they were not, as I knew then, in any way formal members or representatives of KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you liaise in any way between Mr. Rugova, who you mentioned, and the accused on other issues at any time or was there a meeting or did you sort of hold independent meetings with each to liaise on topics or --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It was independent meetings. As I said, there was no meeting where they were both present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: But I -- since our mandate then was to try to find a peaceful settlement, we were preoccupied with or had to look into the situation of the Kosovo Albanian population in Kosovo. And I was discussing with Mr. Rugova what would be his conditions, what would be his desires, what would be the objectives that they wanted fulfilled in order to be able to live within the borders of Yugoslavia under the Yugoslav authority in a peaceful way, and these demands or requests I presented to Mr. Milosevic and vice versa his replies I also did refer to when I spoke to Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to deal with 21, 22, and 23 in an encapsulated form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during your dealings with the accused in these proceedings and your discussions of the Kosovo conflict in the dealings with respect to the Albanians, did you form any impressions about the accused's position in regard to what was most significant to him in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I -- I think Kosovo, to him, was very important because he looked upon it, and he may still look upon it, as the cradle of the Serb culture. There was very little willingness to discuss any kind of autonomy or any kind of -- to go further on any kind of possibility of some kind of self-determination for the Kosovo Albanian people. I did not want, at that time, any new borders in Europe, but I said as chairman in office of the OSCE, I agreed and it was very important for me to say that we should not draw any new borders and I did not want an independent Kosovo. But it was obvious to me that the Kosovo Albanian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. population had to be given much more autonomy when it came to language, culture, et cetera. And this was very difficult for Mr. Milosevic, as I understood, because he felt that that would open up for a secession of Kosovo, and that was totally unacceptable for him. He was very adamant that Kosovo had to be a part of Serbia since that was the cradle of Serb culture and language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you form any impression, quite apart from the one you've just mentioned, about any personal motivation?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I think that this is part of what I also maybe felt in 1993 when I met with Mr. Milosevic at that time, that it is a question of power, but in addition to, as I said, the Kosovo situation, which I think he felt was different from Bosnia and Croatia because of the sentimental feelings attached to Kosovo, I personally saw much of his behaviour as part of his desire for personal power and that he needed a power basis, and he -- that was -- that was part of his -- well, it was -- what shall I say? The reason for his behaviour but also maybe his -- he needed this for his personal power.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I note the time. I believe those are my questions in chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now for half an hour. Ambassador, I must give you the standard warning we have to give to all witnesses: Don't speak to anybody, please, about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Would you be back, please, at half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me how much time I'm going to have, Mr. May, so I'm not surprised by a subsequent decision of yours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That seems to me to be too little, but in view of your practice hitherto, this is nothing new to me. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vollebaek, do you consider, in view of the decision to withdraw the Verification Mission which you yourself took, that you are one of the few people who bear the burden of personal responsibility for the beginning of the war against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, I do not consider that. As I have told you -- and with Your Honours' agreement, I would like to address Mr. Milosevic directly. Because as I told you, Mr. Milosevic, on numerous occasions, that you are responsible. I did that on the 24th of March but I also did it on the 1st of March when we met. You knew what was coming in view of what we had told you. I was in a position that I, for some time, saw the Kosovo Verification Mission having a role, because I saw that it improved the conditions of the population in Kosovo. Then I saw that you had an escalation of military power in Kosovo, which meant that we were faced with a number of incidents, atrocities, that we could not hinder, avoid. And we also had a security risk for our monitors. And in view of that, I had to make the decision to withdraw. But I resisted as long as I could because I first wanted to see if we could avoid a conflict, and also to give you, Mr. Milosevic, a chance to change your mind and cooperate with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's remain within the realm of questions. So do you in fact consider, as it is not in dispute that you yourself personally took the decision, at least in formal sense, do you consider that that decision of yours in fact in the moral and ethical sense is the most weighty because, as you said, you took the personal decision as being the co-chairman for the international conference of the former Yugoslavia and cooperation, the purpose of which was peace. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has dealt with that, I think. Unless there's a new point. If so, perhaps you'd tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the point is that individually, in view of his position as chairman of the Organisation for European Security and Cooperation, that is to say an organisation the purpose of which is European security precisely, which means peace, that in the moral and ethical sense this personal decision is the most difficult. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was it a difficult decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, it was a very difficult decision. It was one of the most difficult decisions I made. But I -- if this implies that I am in any way responsible for the war in Kosovo, I would flatly reject it, Mr. Milosevic, because as, Your Honours, I've told you earlier, we could not perform and fulfil the mandate we were given because Mr. Milosevic's army and paramilitary troops, whatever, did not fulfil their side of the obligation. They had their side of the agreement and were roaming around, making atrocities that we could not stop. And we could not be watching this. So as I see it, the conflict would have -- there was a conflict already. The withdrawal did not start the war. The war was there already when I decided to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I hope you were conscious of the fact that that decision would enable the greatest military machinery that the world has known thus far would be deployed and used against a small country which in nurtured good neighbourly relations with all states surrounding it and which did not jeopardise or threaten any of those countries. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the accused is making statements more than asking questions, but that is nothing new. We have had these type of conversations before, Mr. Milosevic and I. And I think that this is -- it is my view that this is not correct. You will remember, Mr. Milosevic, that the Security Council had passed two Security Council Resolutions, 1160 and 1199. They had been referenced to what is called the Chapter VII language of the UN treaty. And you will know that there had been precedent statements in the Security Council precisely dealing with the risk of regional conflict. It is positively wrong when you say that your attitude, your actions, your behaviour did not threaten the regional stability. We saw that with respect to Macedonia, we saw it with respect to Albania, and we had seen it earlier with respect to the other states in the former Yugoslavia. This had been repeated on and on again. And even though I agree with you that what happened in Kosovo was an internal matter to the sense -- in the sense that what happened inside the borders was an internal matter, it was still a breach of any kind of human rights agreements and, in addition, the OSCE agreement that was the formal basis for the KVM and my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you saying, in fact, that Yugoslavia jeopardised Macedonia or Albanian perhaps?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I am saying that a long time before the 24th of March there were refugees leaving Kosovo in order to avoid the atrocities that were committed by you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did Yugoslavia jeopardise any neighbouring country when you took the decision to withdraw the mission and to enable NATO to unleash the war against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness hadn't said that that happened at all. That wasn't the reason, as you heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, then, sir, Mr. Vollebaek: As a Norwegian originating from a country of the Vikings, valiant warriors, does it seem to be a form of warrior behaviour that a force such as NATO should attack a country with 11 million inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a matter of comment, not a proper question. Ask your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you consider that by withdrawing the mission upon orders from NATO, you in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. That contains an assertion which the witness should deal with. Was the mission withdrawn on the orders of NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer to that question is no. It was -- well, first of all, it was my formal decision. As chairman in office, I had to take the formal decision. It was taken upon an advice by Ambassador Walker, who was the responsible head of the mission, and he told me that he could not any longer take responsibility for the security and safety of the monitors, which I had to take very seriously. Secondly, it was taken in consultation with the other members of the troika of the OSCE, meaning that -- well, Poland was one, and I guess Romania was the other. And in addition to that, in contacts with the members of the Contact Group. But the decision was mine, and there was absolutely no imposition by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You claim that you did not withdraw the mission following orders from NATO to enable the bombing to take place, and now to that you add that NATO didn't even exert any pressure upon you or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. influence you in any way and that you didn't consult NATO at all with respect to the withdrawal of the mission.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I told when the Prosecutor was asking me, I consulted the secretary-general of NATO with respect to if I should try another time to avoid a military conflict. But that was on the 24th of March, after the withdrawal. But the reason for the withdrawal, as I have stated several times, Your Honours, was that we could not fulfil the mission, and we could not have a situation as we had had in Srebrenica where the international community was standing idle, watching atrocities happening. And we saw atrocities happening, and we saw a building up of military force, and that was the situation I was faced with. And this, Your Honours, as I understand this, is the fault of Mr. Milosevic. He was in breach with the agreement. He was told that, and he did not want to comply with the agreement. So in my understanding, he must be responsible for the withdrawal and not anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. That means that you did not withdraw the mission upon NATO's suggestions. I'm now going to read out what was said here by the president of the military NATO committee, General Naumann, a few days ago. He says: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... concerned about the security of the OSCE observers and invited the OSCE to consider NATO's recommendation to withdraw them since we saw that the bombing was imminent." [Interpretation] Full stop there. And the next sentence: [In English] "The OSCE then took the decision to withdraw them I think on the 20th of March."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be placed on the overhead projector. It's taken from the transcript, the LiveNote from this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the chairman of the military committee of NATO says that they called upon the OSCE and recommended to withdraw them "since we saw that the bombing was imminent."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ambassador, you heard it, but perhaps you'd like to have a look and see what the witness said. If you can assist us with it, say so. If not, tell us that. Can you put it on the ELMO, please. It should come up on your screen. If you can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hardly, I'm afraid, but I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Normally, witnesses are not asked to comment on what other witnesses have said, but if you can assist with that since the accused has raised it, perhaps you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour, I don't think that this is in contravention or contradicting what I've said. Of course we were in close touch with NATO, a number of NATO countries, and also NATO as such in the situation that we were having, because NATO was also going to have a role if there would have been a military presence in Kosovo. And we were discussing the military pressure or -- that we were having. This was a part of the discussion before the -- both before the withdrawal but also, of course, before the bombing. As I stated in my replies to the questions asked to me by the Prosecutor, I was under -- I wouldn't call it pressure, but I was asked on repeated occasions to withdraw when it became obvious that we could not fulfil our mandate and when there was a security risk to the members of the monitoring mission. So this -- but I held out as long as I thought that we could do something useful. I think, Your Honours, that the accused is putting this upside-down, actually.
