utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five minutes, Mr. May? You gave me two hours to begin with and then a further 15 minutes. If I have used up one and a half hours until the break and half an hour after the break now, that leaves me at least the 15 minutes that you allotted me a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, did you then believe that old people, women, and children were executed there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. I'm going to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go on from Racak. Now, you've got another ten minutes if you've got any more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have many more questions, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. You've got ten minutes to put them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. I've got used to this kind of treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your statement, among other things, that you could not allow the fact that in the presence of the international forces, something take place that would constitute a crime and which the international forces would stand and watch taking place impotently.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Milosevic. I don't think I used the word "forces" because they were monitors, observers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, how come, from the aspects of your position in 1999 as chairman of the OSCE and your position as foreign minister do you explain and interpret the fact that in the presence of the international forces from June until the end of 1999, over 360.000 non-Albanians were expelled from Kosovo and that tens of thousands of Serb houses were burnt down, and that several thousand people were kidnapped and killed before KFOR's very eyes and that 107 Serbian churches were destroyed all during that time and before the very eyes of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, there must be a question here, but first of all, we will have to ask the ambassador if he can help with this, the position from June 1999 until the -- June 1999 until the end of the year. Can you help us with that, what happened in Kosovo then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from June 1999 until the end of the year, we moved back in, so to say. I mean the international community moved back in, the OSCE moved back in, and we tried to start all over again. We started -- we tried -- the OSCE had, at that time, as its main responsibility, democracy building. We were trying to help in creating various democratic institutions; press, media, the police. That was our task. But it was a very difficult task. We started the police training school. Of course there was absolutely nothing more we wanted than to have everyone moving back to their places, but this was very difficult. And there is no doubt that there were wrongdoings, incidents, criminal acts from the Kosovo Albanian side that we reacted to and protested against. And it was very much against our will that the Serb population were faced with difficulties. As I said, the first thing I did was to go to a Serb monastery, to stay overnight to try to show that we wanted them to stay and that they should be protected. And as you will know, Your Honour, that there still are KFOR soldiers protecting the Serb population. But I -- if I understand Mr. Milosevic correctly, he seems to imply that these wrongdoings undo his own wrongdoings, and I would strongly protest that. And I would again repeat, as I said earlier, that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. if there had been more forthcoming cooperation from Mr. Milosevic's side earlier in that year, all this could have been avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that we accepted the occupation of Kosovo and Yugoslavia in order to avoid having a war break out between NATO and Yugoslavia? Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this reminds me of the 1st of March, 1999. We never talked about an occupation. I talked about a military presence upon your invitation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of my invitation? Well, you asked me to invite you, Yugoslavia to invite you to occupy Yugoslavia? Does that seem to you to be logical, that anybody could do anything like that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I stated several times that I did not mean an occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You call that by a different name. I don't know how to organise my time when I have just a few more minutes left, but at the start of your statement, you said that in 1993, you came to see me, to ask me to use my influence with the Srpska Krajina and the leadership of Srpska Krajina to support your proposal for negotiations to take place in Norway and that those negotiations did in fact take place; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you have any knowledge of any international or internal initiative for achieving peace which Serbia and I personally did not support throughout all those years?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I'm in a position to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, in addition to the explanations you gave, you explained one point that seems to me to be absolutely fantastic, to hear it and to comment on it, and it is this: It would appear that we supported those peace efforts - and let me say that we supported all peace efforts and peace was the only issue we dealt with when it came to Croatia and Bosnia - in order that Croatia could not go to war on two fronts and not in order to achieve peace between Republika Srpska and Republic of Srpska Krajina. And you even said that Serbia -- the Serbs should cease their military operations against Croatia. Now, as you were in Zagreb at the time, do you know that in 1993, for example, and even much before that, there were no military operations on the part of Serbs against Croatia but that they banned access to their territory, the territory in which they had been living for several centuries and that that operation of theirs was called at the time colloquially "the log revolution." As you know, logs are not of an offensive means. So do you know that there were no military operations by the Serbs against Croatia at that time when you were in Zagreb? Are you aware of that? Do you know that that was so?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am prepared to answer questions relating to the meeting I had with Mr. Milosevic in 1993, but I find it difficult to answer this question. I did not, Mr. Milosevic, go into any kind of definition of military action between the government of Croatia and the Krajina Republic in 1993 because this was not the question I was asked when I answered the question about the meeting you and I had. The question I was asked was whether I had met you before I met you as a foreign minister, and I told about that. What I felt was important for this process that you now deal with, namely the Kosovo crisis, was your attitude toward Muslims, because I vividly remember, maybe because I still have bad conscience for not strongly protesting what you said, that you said that we -- you would assist me. There were -- probably we cannot call it a war then if that's according to your wish, we can drop that terminology, but there were military activities that made the government of Croatia busy in trying to fend off the Serbs in Krajina at the same time as there was fighting going on with the Muslims in Bosnia. And I very well remember that you said that you would tell the -- or advise the Serbs in Knin to go to Norway to go on with the negotiations precisely because you thought it was proper for the Croats to fight the Muslims. And as I said earlier today, you told me that -- and your words -- I'm still quite sure that the words were, "Mr. Vollebaek, you have to agree with me we cannot have a Muslim republic in Europe." And of course I should have stopped you there. I did not. So I did not accept your statement but I did not protest strongly either, which I suppose I should have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vollebaek -- Mr. Vollebaek, as you know very well, the number of Muslims living in Yugoslavia, and as you know full well that not a single one of them all time during those crises and wars were mistreated, expelled, killed or arrested in Serbia, and as you know full well that we cooperated and had over 70.000 Muslim refugees in Serbia from Bosnia-Herzegovina, that we cooperated with different Muslim enclaves such as the one in Bihac region to which we sent flour and corn and food generally, the one that got the most number of votes for the president of Bosnia, Fikret Avdic, that's where he came from, as you know all this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question? The witness -- the witness says that is what you said. So any argument is not to the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is precisely unbelievable and impossible, because we never spoke about a Muslim state, rather, the endeavours that were being made to create a Muslim extremist state. And if you recall, I mentioned to you on the occasion exclusively Muslim extremists. I spoke about Muslim extremists and not Muslims, because the vast large portion of Serbian inhabitants are Muslims. And I quoted Izetbegovic's declaration - and I don't have to quote it, it has been published in book form - in which Izetbegovic says that among the Muslim religion and non-Muslim societies and institutions, there cannot be peaceful coexistence. I spoke to you about the danger of Islamic fundamentalism, and that has been proven to be true, because over 6.000 Mujahedin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just stop for a moment. Let the witness answer. What is being put, Mr. Vollebaek, is that what the accused spoke to you about was Muslim extremism and Muslim fundamentalism. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that the word "extremist" or "fundamentalist" was used. I know the word "Muslim republic" was used but I do not recall that the word "extremist" was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: More specifically, Ambassador, I understand Mr. Milosevic to be saying that he did not say to you that, "We cannot have a Muslim state in Europe."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear him saying that also. My recollection from that conversation, and I have gone over that several times in my memory, is that he said "a Muslim republic in Europe."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One more question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult for me, Mr. May, to ask just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you not think that today - and I'm asking you, Mr. Vollebaek - in especially in light of Clinton's statement prior to the bombing of Yugoslavia, which justifies -- which he justifies by the alleged massacres in Racak and mentions the civilians, women, children, and so on and so forth, and you know that none of that is true, that this was a fabrication in a very dirty way, a reason for war, a pretext for war and aggression which NATO launched against a European country, in this case against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and created -- which led to very serious consequences? So do you not think that this is a fabrication, especially as throughout the world it has been assessed that this event in Racak was abused for those purposes? And what Clinton stated on that occasion has been seen not to be true now and was in fact a pretext. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not certain what I'm going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was Racak used as a pretext for the NATO bombing and, as it's alleged, aggression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, not. Racak took place on the 15th or 16th of January, 15th of January. The bombing started on the 21st of March. We had a number of incidents that took place afterwards. And Racak took place. I suppose that I have not heard anyone, Mr. Milosevic, to kind of pretend that this was a kind of setup, that someone put people there to be killed in order to have a NATO bombing. That's the first time I hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me just to quote, please, just Clinton's words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've been over this. Now, Mr. Wladimiroff, have you any questions of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, please. I should like to quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. You've had your time. You have had rather more than you have. Much of it has been spent arguing. Now, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Wladimiroff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, in your testimony, you told the Court about your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. meetings with the accused, and when you were asked about the role of the accused when military affairs were discussed, you told the Court that military or generals were present on the Yugoslav side. You also testified that the accused discussed these issues and made decisions. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the military not participate in these discussions? And I mean the military on the Yugoslav side. Or did they participate?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I do not recall that they participated actively. They -- I -- on my side, I normally spoke, and on Mr. Milosevic's side, it was normally he that spoke. We had at least, as I recall, on the 21st of January there was a -- an intermission or it was a break, and the Yugoslav side withdrew, I suppose for consultations. But in my presence, as I recall it, they rarely spoke. Maybe they answered precise questions about something, but I remember that my conversation was with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were there military on your part?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. I do not recall everyone that was participating. I think normally we had only civilians, but there might have been some military advisors. I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they participate in the conversation or was it you who did the discussing?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I did the talking with Mr. Milosevic. As I said, it was more or less he and I. I might also ask for some clarification, probably, but the direct conversation was between Mr. Milosevic and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself an expert on military affairs or were these conversations on a more superficial level that didn't need any specific military knowledge so you could do it yourself, Milosevic could do it himself?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I am absolutely no military expert, and we had mainly, I would say, political discussions. But some of the political issues were based, then, on what were kind of military issues since there were incidents that happened. But I think that most of these issues could be dealt with without having a lot of military knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I come back to the telephone conversation of the 24th of March, 1999. You told the Court that the Rambouillet talks had broken up, and you were heading off society with having an armed conflict. You told the Court you had a conversation with Solana, the Secretary-General of NATO. You did not tell the Court what this conversation was about. Can you tell the Court what Solana told you?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I do not recall the conversation as such, but I, in this period, after the withdrawal of the KVM, I saw things deteriorating, and as the NATO foreign minister, I was informed about the discussions in NATO about a possible armed intervention from the NATO side. I felt it was my duty to try to avoid this in my capacity as chairman of the OSCE, and I had a number of discussions with my advisors, with the troika, if there was anything that we could do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's not what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, but I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is do you remember what Solana told you?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I asked him if it was okay for me to call Mr. Milosevic and tell him that there was another chance, if NATO would agree to start over again if Mr. Milosevic would agree to do so. And his answer was yes, he supported the conversation I had with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your call with Mr. Milosevic, you passed this message from Solana to Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I don't think I passed a message from Solana, but this was a message from the chairman of the OSCE to Mr. Milosevic. But I suppose that I also told him that I could make my influence in NATO so that I could go back to NATO and say I had this conversation with Milosevic, he was willing to talk to us, he was willing to cooperate, and that would have an impact in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A technical question. May I ask the witness a technical question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wanted to ask him whether he's sure he talked to me on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nothing re-arising. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will ask the question which was put at the end. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you sure that you spoke to Mr. Milosevic on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, when you are on a telephone conversation, I suppose there are certain limits to what you can be assured sure of. But I recognised his voice, and I was told that I was put through to Mr. Milosevic, and I had people in my office witnessing the conversation. There's even a report in the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs from the conversation. Well, I assumed. I assumed up until today that I spoke to him on the 24th of March, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. No. We've taken this as far as we can. Ambassador, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded. I'm sorry. Judge Robinson had a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ambassador, earlier you, in commenting on the statement that you attributed to Mr. Milosevic, that he said that, "We cannot have a Muslim republic in Europe," you say that you regretted not having answered him immediately. Would you explain that regret.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I thought that this was a statement that violated my sense of human rights because it was made, as I understood it at that time, as a statement against one group of people in general, and specifically in Europe. And that was the reason why I thought that I should have protested or told him that I disagreed with him. However, at that time, I didn't feel that it was the place for such a discussion of principle because we were in a hurry to avoid a conflict in another part of the former Yugoslavia, and I needed him to put pressure on the Serbs in Knin. So that's why I did not at that time do what I otherwise would have done, namely said that I disagreed with his attitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're waiting for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, while we're waiting for the next witness to resume - I understand that Mr. Saxon will resume - I wonder if I might raise one issue concerning Mr. Crosland, who is on our witness list to testify on Wednesday, circumstances and timing permitting. My note is that on the 29th of May, we applied and indicated that we wanted to have Mr. Crosland bis'd in part, and that statement was provided to the Chamber on the 29th. In view of the fact that he will be testifying in a day or two, I wonder whether the Court might review that and give me an indication at your convenience so that I know whether to prepare him for a live witness or for a 92 bis. I have a summary now for a live one, but I would have to change the summary to a bis witness. That's the only thing I want to raise as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is going to give evidence next after this witness? Who is coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness K25. Mr. Nice will be handling it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll certainly look at the evidence of Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, thank you for coming back. Your evidence, of course, is subject to the same declaration that you made on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Saxon: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, on Friday before we broke, we were discussing the creation of what you refer to as the joint staff or joint command for Kosovo which met in Pristina on a weekly basis starting in 1998. And you also told the Trial Chamber about the formation of similar municipal staffs in the various different municipalities around Kosovo. I'd like to show you some documents, if I may, and we'll start with what is referred to as the OTP Exhibit number -- reference number K1280 if I could ask the usher's assistance, please, to distribute copies around the courtroom and place one on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps if the -- perhaps if a copy of the English version could be placed on the ELMO so that everyone watching can follow along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Aliu, if I could direct your attention, please, to the first page of the Serbian version. Can you find that, please?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the Serbian copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document. It says: "To Defence Departments/Sections," in large letters. It's dated apparently 28th of July, it looks to be 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And first of all, I'd like to draw your attention to the bottom of that page that you're looking at. Do you see a signature at the bottom of that page, Mr. Aliu? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there's a signature at the foot of the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the signature of the chief of the defence secretariat, Petar Ilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the man who was your supervisor for a number of years during the 1990s; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This was the man who was my chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we can just take a look at the text on this page. It starts out -- it says: "Subject: Instructions for the defence of inhabited areas." And then the first paragraph begins: "The joint command for Kosovo and Metohija has issued instructions for the defence of inhabited areas from the activities of Siptar terrorists which also prescribe the obligations of the SMO and its organisational units: the defence administration, departments and sections." This joint command that is being referred to in this document, is this the same joint command for Kosovo that you talked to us about on Friday?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's that command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then further down on the same page, it says the following: "We would point out that the joint command for Kosovo and Metohija has determined a new composition of municipal defence staffs and in addition to representatives of local self-governed units, the MUP, the SO, the IO, and the VJ, chiefs of defence departments and heads of defence sections have also become members of these staffs." Can you explain to the Court which are the municipal defence staffs that are being discussed here?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the commands of the staffs or sections in the municipalities of Kosova, and there are 28 of them. In these commands of the municipal staffs, leaders of the sections or the municipal secretariats were supposed to join up as members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just as on Friday you described -- you told the Trial Chamber of a number of persons who were members of the joint staff for the province of Kosovo. According to this document, would representatives of similar institutions and organisations be members of the joint staff -- joint staffs - excuse me - at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were not members of the joint -- members of the joint staff. The members of the joint staff were only those people I listed on Friday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think my question wasn't clear. The people who you listed on Friday were, according to your testimony, members of the joint staff for the province of Kosovo that met in Pristina. In this document, we see Petar Ilic talking about or pointing out, to use Petar Ilic's language, that the joint command for Kosovo and Metohija has determined a new composition of municipal defence staffs. And then Petar Ilic goes on to explain which institutions those members might represent. My question simply is: From this document, are you able to tell whether the composition of the municipal defence staffs, in terms of the different institutions that were represented on the municipal defence staffs, were roughly similar to the different institutions represented on the joint command for Kosovo as a whole?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These staffs were merely for the municipalities, and these joint staff were appointed by municipal assemblies, and these municipal assemblies were made up besides the municipal staff like the municipal chairman, people like the chairman of the secretariat or the defence section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And who would these municipal staffs respond to?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These responded to the municipal assemblies and the chairmen of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And maybe I can impose on the usher again. I'm sorry. Perhaps you could remain at the ELMO again for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could turn to the very next page. If you could look at it on the ELMO as well. The very next page says, at the top, "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," and then it says, "Instructions for the Defence of Inhabited Places." And then we see the word "(Temporary)," and then in the middle of the page, it says, "July 1998." Do you see that language?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why that word "Temporary" is there?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's temporary because the units that operated in the zones mentioned knew that they would -- later they would be sent back to where they worked before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- and at what point would these individuals be sent back to where they were before? What was going on at the time that required the issuance of temporary instructions?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These temporary instructions were issued to all the secretariats and defence departments to carrying out -- from carrying out their military duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were instructions such as these issued during times of war or crisis?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In times of war and in times of crisis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you could turn the page again to what is on page 3 of the English version. I'm not sure which page it is on your version. But you'll see the number 2 followed by a small "a". Do you see that subsection, Mr. Aliu? Section 2a. Do you see that? That section is entitled, "The Composition and Tasks of the Civil Protection and Systems for Monitoring and Reporting." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you -- if we go to the next page, on the English version page 4, there is the number 1 in the middle of page 4 and the following text appears: "General purpose CZ," which I believe stands for Civilian Protection Units, "administer first aid, rescue people from ruins, extinguish initial and smaller fires, clear barricades, organise the washing of streets, etc." Is this a fair description of the activities of Civilian Protection Units during times of war and crisis in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. These are Civil Protection Units whose duties were, in fact, first aid, saving people from ruins and from fire. And in times of war -- or in 1990, they later -- they were armed, although they were forbidden to carry arms under the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn the page again. On page 5 of the English version we see, about halfway down the page, the number 3, and we see a line that says, in capital letters: "The Task and Grouping of Forces." And if we scan down that section to the -- to the fifth paragraph in that section, there is a phrase at the very end of that paragraph that I want to ask you about. You see a phrase there that says "and continuity of commanding." Do you see that phrase, Mr. Aliu?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the fifth page? I can't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be on the 6th page.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of your -- the fifth paragraph after the number 3. At the end of the paragraph, we see the words "and continuity of commanding."

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 3. Please, can you ask the question again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you see these words "continuity of commanding"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's fifth paragraph on page 6. Page 6 of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at page 6, the fifth paragraph down, the last words in that paragraph say, in English, "continuity of commanding." Do you see that? "Neprekidnost komandovanja." I apologise for my horrible Serbian. Do you see those words, Mr. Aliu?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those words that you mention are not here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you look at page 6 and you look at this paragraph - and perhaps the usher can help me - look at the last two words in that paragraph. Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the last two words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what does principle or idea of continuity of commanding means?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means continuing all the operations, all the duties, and keeping them going until they are completely performed, until all these military duties have been performed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would military units be able to function in wartime without continuity of command?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they would not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could, please, take a look at the very last paragraph on the same page, Mr. Aliu, where the text says the following: "The forces for operations inside the town are primarily determined by demographic composition. In ethnically clean Serbian settlements and zones, the organisation of defence is easier, while in mixed ones it is complex and has to be organised by apartment blocks. If that is not possible, then citizens should be evacuated into the ethnically clean zones." Do you see what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, when this passage talks about citizens being evacuated into ethnically clean zones, which citizens is it talking about, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is only about evacuating Serbian citizens, who were very few Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in number. And they had to be evacuated into areas with a mainly Serbian population, whereas in Serbian populated areas, they were totally secure and there was no need for any evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And if you could also, please, turn to -- I believe it's on the next page. You'll see the letter 5, and you'll see the word "Commanding" in large letters. And in the second paragraph on that page, we see the following: "The staff functionally ties together and unites all the defence structures (the VJ reserve, the MUP, the CZ --" or the civilian protection -- "enterprises and citizens) as 'the MUP reserve.'" Can we take from this passage that the joint staff for Kosovo or for each municipality ties together and unites all the different defence structures and units that would be mobilised during wartime?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would now tender, Your Honours, that document into evidence. That document could be removed now from the ELMO and from the witness's table.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 245.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will have to depend once again on Mr. Usher for another document. This is a document that has OTP reference number K1282. And again if the Serbian version could be handed to the witness and the English version placed on the ELMO, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document of which the date is unclear, at least in the English translation. 28 July nineteen nine something, from the Pristina defence administration.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is from 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1998. Thank you. It's addressed to the chiefs of --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll look at it. First of all, can you take a look at the signature again, Mr. Aliu? It's on the document. You might have to turn the page. Can you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Petar Ilic's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we go back to the first page, the document is addressed to the chiefs of defence departments and heads of defence sections. And below that, from 1 to 29. And then in the first paragraph, it says: "Pursuant to the Instructions on the Defence of Inhabited Areas issued by the joint command for Kosovo and Metohija, and with the objective of the engagement of Civilian Protection and Monitoring and Reporting Service personnel and performance of their tasks, I hereby issue the following." And then we see the word "Order" and a series of paragraphs after that. My question for you is if you can just briefly explain, who is Petar Ilic providing orders to, and based on what?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this document, the head of the provincial defence secretariat, Petar Ilic, is giving orders to all the communal staff, all the municipal staffs in all the territory of Kosova. And he also gives an order to the monitoring and reporting service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says in the very first line: "Pursuant to the Instructions on the Defence of Inhabited Areas issued by the Joint Command." Are those orders pursuant to the instructions that we looked at a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the orders that we were looking at a short time ago and the tasks facing the municipal staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would now offer this document into evidence, please, and I would ask Ms. Graham if she would help me with --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 246.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next document has OTP reference number K1283.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, if you could take a look at this document, please. It's dated the 30th of July, 1998, Pristina. Do you recognise the signature at the end of this document? Take a look at the back page, please.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very back page. Take a look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature is the same person. It's Petar Ilic, the head of the defence secretariat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would go back to the first page, please. The document is addressed to "Regional Organ of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Cekic personally, Belgrade." And below that, it says, "Guidelines for the defence of inhabited areas issued by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." Below that, we see extract from the guidelines referring to the obligations of the Federal Ministry of Defence. Who is Petar Ilic sending this information to?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's sending this information to the Serbian defence authorities in Belgrade and refers once again to the guidelines of the Defence of inhabited areas and states that it's been issued by the joint command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was brought -- this is about the orders being issued by the joint command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just a quick question.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. This document is encoded and is very urgent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aliu. Just to move more quickly, the Federal Ministry of Defence that received this message from Mr. Ilic, was this office the superior of Mr. Ilic?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Mr. Ilic's superior authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would now offer this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 247.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have one more document I'd like to show the witness. This document has OTP reference number K2685.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, you might want to turn the page and look actually at the second page of the document. This document is dated 2 November 1998. It is also signed by Mr. Petar Ilic on the last page. On page 2, we see it's directed to the Federal Ministry of Defence, sector for civilian defence, to Lieutenant General Geza Farkas personally, Belgrade. And then it says in the first and second paragraphs: "... we would like to inform you of the following: "- in our communication strictly confidential no. 80-10/3, we requested the Command of the 3rd Army to secure for us arms and ammunition for all the units that are being formed and developed by the departments and sections on the territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija as follows: civil defence detachments - for 1.665 military conscripts, communications units - 423, Monitoring and Reporting - 1.179, civilian protection - 3.365 members, or a total of 6.632." Mr. Aliu, during 1998, while you were still working in the Civilian Protection Unit, did members of that unit receive arms?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you a detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to answer my question, Mr. Aliu.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very quickly, yes. Yes. They received weapons, and I myself saw members of the Civilian Protection Units being armed by members of the army. And you can see here very clearly that the Civilian Protection Units here are armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, did all of the members of the Civilian Protection Units receive arms?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the ranks of the Civil Protection Units received weapons. And in the municipal assemblies and the municipal secretariats, they all received weapons. And that's what I said on the first day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, did Serbs and Albanians receive weapons?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Albanians never received weapons. And indeed, they were all disarmed in 1987 and had to pay large sums in compensation. And these were only levelled against the Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1998, did you ever see weapons brought to Kosovo and distributed? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the defence secretariat, in the command of the Army Corps, and the arms were submitted by a man named Delibasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were the weapons brought there?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were brought in trucks to the command and then they were distributed from the command, it seems to me, in small chests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did these trucks belong to?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trucks belonged to the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the weapons being unloaded and distributed?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kinds of weapons were distributed?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatic rifles and semi-automatics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these weapons distributed to?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would now tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 248.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And my last question for this witness -- my last two questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, did your boss, Petar Ilic, ever tell you what might happen to the Albanian population in Kosovo if attacks by Albanian terrorists escalated there?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the number of attacks by Albanians increased -- they weren't terrorist attacks, I must say, they were merely protecting their own homes -- if they happened, all the Albanians would have to go to Albania across the Accursed Mountains. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I have nothing further for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was told that there was a matter of concern about a protected witness, K32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, not that I know of. If there is, we will deal with it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Mr. Aliu, could you be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow morning. I think I'm right. I will be informed by the registrar if that's the time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Nine o'clock, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Nine o'clock tomorrow morning. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just some technical questions, Mr. May. You needn't worry. The instructions for the defence of settlements, there's no end to that. Now, is that a mistake? In my copy, the copy I have received -- or doesn't it have an end to it? Because these other documents, the other papers, I see that they were interviewed and they had signatures. I'm talking about this thickest document. There's no end to it. It ends with page 13, the copy I have, without a signature. Now, I'm just asking whether you can provide me with the complete document. That's my first question. And secondly, are there any changes in the order of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is to say, the schedule and list that I have received, the latest one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, can you deal with the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll try, Your Honour. To the best of my knowledge, Your Honour, this is the complete document or it is the most complete version in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor, but I will check just to make sure that no mistake has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Nice, you said the next witness would be K25?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then following him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Crosland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Crosland.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think, with the short day, that's all we've got time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've got, what, two days left. I think they're normal short days, 9.00 until quarter to two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope the evidence will fill the time and I'm not sure that we can have a reserve, but I'll just check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We will adjourn now.
